sentences: I grew up in Iloilo, in a little wooden house beside the river.
My father built it himself with timber left over from the boats he repaired.
It stood on tall posts, because every rainy season the river crept under the floor.
When I was small, I thought the water was a friendly neighbor visiting us.
We had two rooms, a kitchen at the back, and a bamboo porch.
All six children slept in one room, lined up on mats like sardines.
My mother hung a mosquito net over us, and it smelled of smoke and soap.
In the morning the sun came through the gaps and drew stripes on the floor.
I used to count those stripes before anyone else woke up.
The kitchen was my mother's kingdom, with a clay stove and a blackened pot.
She woke before dawn to cook rice and prepare the cakes she sold at market.
The smell of coconut milk and sticky rice pulled us all out of bed.
My father kept his tools under the house, wrapped in old flour sacks.
There were chisels, planes, and a heavy mallet that I was never allowed to touch.
Sometimes I sat on a bucket and watched him shape a plank into a boat.
He whistled while he worked, always the same slow tune about a fisherman and the moon.
Our mango tree stood in front, and my brother Nestor climbed it like a monkey.
In April the fruit turned golden, and the whole street argued over the first ripe one.
We also kept three chickens, one pig, and a rooster named General who hated me.
Every morning he chased me to the well, and every morning I screamed.
Four families shared the well, and all the gossip of the street was traded there.
I carried water in a dented tin pail, and my arms ached all the way home.
When the typhoon season came, the sky turned the color of an old bruise.
The wind rattled the tin roof so loudly that we could not hear each other.
My mother lit a candle before a picture of the Holy Child, and we prayed.
My father tied the boats tight to the posts and checked the knots again and again.
One night the river rose so high that it touched our first step.
We climbed to the little attic and ate cold rice with dried fish by candlelight.
I was frightened, but my sister Luz told ghost stories until we laughed instead.
In the morning the water went down and left brown mud on everything.
We scrubbed the floor with coconut husks, and it smelled of wet earth for a week.
After supper the neighbors gathered on our porch to talk and share palm wine.
We children chased fireflies along the riverbank with empty jam jars.
My grandmother sat in her rocking chair, chewing betel nut and humming old songs.
She had a face like a dried mango, but her eyes were bright and quick.
She taught me to sew on a button, and that small skill carried me through life.
The house had no electricity until I was nine, so we lived by oil lamps.
When the first bulb glowed in our kitchen, my mother cried and my father laughed at her.
I think of that house almost every day, even now in Abu Dhabi.
Sometimes I close my eyes and hear the river slapping against the posts.
I can smell the rice cakes and feel the warm bamboo under my bare feet.
It was a poor house, but it was full of music and noise and love.
The dish that brings everything back for me is my mother's chicken adobo.
She cooked it on Sundays, when my father came home early from the water.
I can still see the black iron pot on the clay stove, its lid rattling.
First she crushed a whole head of garlic with the flat of her knife.
Then she poured in vinegar and soy sauce, with dried bay leaves and black pepper.
The vinegar was made from coconut sap, sharp and a little sweet.
She never measured anything, and when I asked how much, she said enough.
For years that answer made me furious, because I wanted to be a good cook.
Now I understand that enough is a real measurement, and it lives in your hands.
While the chicken simmered, we children hung around the stove like hungry cats.
Nestor was the worst, because he lifted the lid every five minutes.
My mother tapped his fingers with a wooden spoon, and he yelped as if burned.
We ate together on the porch, on a long bench my father made from a boat plank.
My mother served the rice first, a mountain of it, steaming in the morning light.
Then she spooned the dark sauce over the top, and the rice drank it up.
There was never enough chicken for everyone, so the sauce was the real treasure.
My father always gave me the thigh and winked, as if it were our secret.
I think he knew I was the thin one who forgot to eat when reading.
Afterward we had sliced green mango with salt, and it made our eyes water happily.
The adobo tasted even better the next day, once the flavors had settled.
My mother said that was the secret of life, because some things improve when left alone.
When I moved to Abu Dhabi, I packed a small bottle of that coconut vinegar.
It leaked on my best blue blouse, and the whole airplane smelled like a Filipino kitchen.
The first time I made adobo in my new kitchen, I cried into the pot.
It tasted close, but not quite right, because the memory was missing.
Ramon laughed and said it was perfect, but he was being kind.
Over the years I found the right vinegar in a supermarket near our building.
Now my daughter Liza asks for my adobo after every long shift at the hospital.
She sits at my table in her blue uniform and eats three plates in silence.
I tell her that is exactly how I looked at my mother's table.
My son Paolo wants extra sauce and a fried egg, which my mother would never allow.
I let him, because sons and grandchildren are allowed things that daughters never were.
Sometimes I use a pressure cooker now, and I feel a little guilty.
My mother's pot was never in a hurry, and her adobo carried that patience.
On tired days I put on the rice and chop the garlic slowly.
The smell comes up, and suddenly I am eight years old on that bamboo porch.
I can hear the river, the rooster, and my brothers fighting over the last fish.
A single dish can carry a whole house inside it, with its people and weather.
That is the kind of memory no restaurant can sell you.
I believe that is why we cook for the people we love.
When I am gone, I hope my children will stand at the stove and say enough.
Then they will smile, and I will be there in the steam.
My school days began at six, in a one-story school near the Iloilo market.
It had a red tin roof, a flagpole, and a yard that turned to soup in rain.
I walked there barefoot with my two sisters, carrying books tied with rubber strap.
My mother ironed my white blouse every Sunday night with an iron full of hot coals.
She polished my one pair of black shoes, and I carried them in a cloth bag.
At the gate I put them on, because a student should look like a student.
Our first teacher was Missus Dayrit, a round woman with a voice like a church bell.
She had a long wooden pointer that she used only on the blackboard and the occasional fly.
We sat three to a desk, on benches worn smooth by generations.
I loved the smell of chalk dust and the squeak of the wiped board.
We learned to write in copybooks with blue lines and a rooster on the cover.
My handwriting was neat, and Missus Dayrit pinned my page on the wall.
I was so proud that I tripped over a goat on the way home.
Every morning we stood in rows, sang the anthem, and stretched our arms wide.
Then we recited the multiplication tables, and the sound rolled across the yard like waves.
Arithmetic was my best subject, but stories were what I loved most.
Missus Dayrit also taught us to sing, mostly songs about rain and rice.
The school library was one shelf in a cupboard that smelled of mildew.
I read every book on it twice, even a thick one about the stars.
At lunchtime we sat under the acacia tree and opened our tin boxes of rice.
A boy named Jun always traded his dried fish for my sweet rice cake.
On rainy days the teacher let us tell stories, and those were my favorite afternoons.
I discovered then that people listened to me if I used my hands.
Of course I also got into trouble, as every child does.
Once I drew the principal with a fish for a nose on my notebook.
My friend Tess laughed so hard that she fell off the bench.
We were both sent to stand in the corner.
Standing there, I felt terrible, but I also felt a small thrill of rebellion.
My mother heard about it that evening and gave me a look worse than any scolding.
Then she laughed, because she never could stay angry with me for long.
At the school fiesta we staged a play about a girl who saved her village.
I was the girl, with a crown of banana leaves and a cape made from a curtain.
I forgot my lines in the middle, so I made up new ones, and the audience clapped.
That was the day I decided I wanted to stand in front of a room and talk.
The war had left some of our books torn, and the walls were patched with plywood.
We had little, but our teachers treated every child as a future doctor.
They gave us the gift of believing we could be somebody, and never charged a peso.
When I became a teacher myself, I tried to give that same gift to every child.
Even now, when I smell chalk, I am six years old again with tight braids.
In the dry months we played tag until the dust turned our uniforms brown.
I would go back for one more morning with the anthem and the tables.
My dearest friend when I was young was a girl called Teresita, but everyone called her Tess.
She lived four houses away, in a blue shack with a mango tree in the yard.
We met when I was seven, the day she fell into the river.
I fished her out with a bamboo pole, though the water only reached her waist.
She screamed beautifully anyway, and afterward she said I had saved her life.
I never denied it, because it made me feel like a hero.
Tess was small and quick, with a gap in her teeth and scabbed knees.
She could whistle through that gap better than any boy in the neighborhood.
Every afternoon we collected shells along the riverbank and traded them like coins.
She taught me to catch crabs with a string and a piece of fish head.
I taught her to read, using labels from tin cans because her house had no books.
Her mother sold fish at the market, and her hands always smelled of salt.
Tess was embarrassed by that smell, but I told her I loved it.
On Saturdays we helped our mothers, and afterward we made dolls from corn husks.
Tess was the better artist, and she drew tiny faces with a burnt matchstick.
My dolls always looked angry, so we pretended they were the teachers.
Under the big mango tree, the roots made a secret little room.
We kept a biscuit tin there, filled with shells, a blue marble, and a letter.
We promised to open the tin when we were old women.
Tess wanted to be a singer, and she practiced with a coconut shell for a microphone.
I wanted to be a teacher, and I practiced on her with great success.
When we were twelve, her family moved to Bacolod, where her uncle had found work.
I remember the morning they left, with their belongings piled on a truck.
Tess stood at the back and waved her scarf until it turned the corner.
I ran after it for a block and lost one slipper.
For months afterward the riverbank felt empty, and even the shells seemed dull.
We wrote letters for a while, with drawings in the margins and pressed flowers inside.
Then life grew busy, the letters came less often, and finally they stopped.
It is a small sadness that I carry quietly, like a stone in a pocket.
Years later, when I was already teaching, I received a postcard with a picture of a stage.
On the back she wrote that she had become a singer after all, but only in church.
I laughed and cried at once, because that was exactly right.
I never learned whether she opened the tin under the mango tree.
When I visited Iloilo again, the tree was gone, and a concrete house stood there.
I stood on the pavement for a long time, feeling foolish and tender.
Now I sing in my own church choir in Abu Dhabi, and sometimes I think of her.
When the sopranos reach a high note, I imagine her whistling through that gap.
A childhood friend knows the girl you were before you learned to be careful.
Tess knew me when I was brave, silly, and barefoot.
If she ever hears this story, I want her to know I kept the blue marble.
I keep it in a dish beside my sewing box, and it catches the morning light.
Good friends can be lost without ever really being lost.
I believe she is out there somewhere, still singing.
My first real job was in a dressmaker's shop called Madame Lim's, in Iloilo.
I was sixteen, and I worked there on Saturdays to help pay for my books.
The shop was a long narrow room, hot as an oven, with ten sewing machines.
Madame Lim was not really a madame, but she liked the title because it sounded elegant.
She was a tiny woman with a measuring tape draped around her neck like a scarf.
She wore thick glasses, and she could spot a crooked seam from across the room.
My first task was to sort buttons, with a huge biscuit tin in my lap.
There were thousands of them, in brass and mother of pearl and every color of plastic.
I thought it was the most boring work in the world.
But Madame Lim said a person who cannot sort buttons cannot be trusted with scissors.
After three weeks she let me sew hems, and I felt promoted to queen.
The fabrics were wonderful, with pink satin for weddings and crisp cotton for school uniforms.
I loved the smell of new cloth and the soft sound of the shears.
My fingers were pricked a hundred times, and I learned to suck away the blood.
Madame Lim paid me fifteen pesos a week, which seemed like a fortune.
I gave ten to my mother and kept five, and with it I bought a small mirror.
My coworkers were four older women who gossiped from morning to night and fed me sweet bread.
Aling Pacita sang old love songs and cried a little at every high note.
Young Remedios was getting married, and we all stitched her wedding gown together.
It took two months, and I sewed three hundred tiny pearl beads along the neckline.
On the wedding day I peeked into the church and saw the dress glowing.
I felt a deep, private pride, because my stitches were holding that bride together.
That job taught me patience, because you cannot rush a seam or hide a mistake.
It also taught me about people, because customers told their whole lives while being measured.
I learned that a woman standing in her slip will say anything.
Madame Lim taught me to look closely and to be honest, even when the cloth was expensive.
She said a good dress is a kindness, because it helps a person feel brave.
One afternoon a rich lady complained that her blouse was too tight.
Madame Lim calmly let out the seam and told her the blouse had been perfect.
I learned that sometimes diplomacy is a form of tailoring.
During the typhoon season the roof leaked, and we covered the fabric with plastic sheets.
I worked there for two years, until I went to teachers college.
On my last day Madame Lim gave me silver scissors wrapped in a handkerchief.
She said a teacher also cuts and sews, only with words and children.
I still have those scissors, and they sit in my sewing box in Abu Dhabi.
Every time I make a dress for my granddaughter, I think of that hot little room.
My fingers still remember how to hold a needle without looking.
Not every first job is glamorous, but a good one teaches you how to begin.
I sometimes tell my students that even sorting buttons can be the start of something great.
They usually laugh, but I mean every word.
That tiny shop made me patient, careful, and proud of ordinary work.
I would walk back into it tomorrow, with a biscuit tin in my lap.
The most important person in my life is my husband Ramon.
I was twenty-two and teaching my first class in a village school outside Iloilo.
He was twenty-five, a ship's cook, home on leave after a long voyage.
We met at church on a rainy Sunday, with everyone crowded under the porch roof.
I was holding my father's huge black umbrella, which was broken on one side.
Ramon stood next to me, soaked to the skin, and said my umbrella looked brave.
I told him it was only stubborn, and he laughed so loudly the priest turned around.
He walked me home that afternoon, carrying the umbrella and describing the places he had seen.
He had been to Hamburg, Rotterdam, and Singapore, and he remembered the food in each.
I had never left the island, so I listened as if to fairy tales.
What I noticed first were his hands, big and burned by the kitchen.
Those were the hands of a man who feeds people, and I trusted them at once.
He courted me for two years, writing from ports all over the world on thin blue paper.
Each letter smelled faintly of cinnamon and diesel, and I kept them in a shoebox.
When he came home he cooked for my whole family, and my mother approved after one plate.
My father was harder to please, but Ramon fixed a leaking boat for him, and that settled it.
We married in the same church where we met, on a bright morning in March.
My hands shook so badly that I dropped the ring.
Ramon picked it up and said it was a sign we would never lose each other.
Life with a seafarer is not easy, because he is always leaving or arriving.
For nearly thirty years our marriage was a series of airport goodbyes and joyful homecomings.
I raised the children mostly alone, and I learned to fix a roof and argue with a landlord.
Ramon sent money and long letters, and later recorded tapes of his voice telling bedtime stories.
Liza and Paolo listened to those tapes until the ribbon wore thin.
When he was home he took over the kitchen, and the flat smelled of garlic and ginger.
He is a gentle man who never raises his voice, not even about a crashed motorbike.
He just sat down on the step and asked the boy how he planned to pay.
When the ships grew old and he grew tired, he retired and came home for good.
It was strange at first, because we had spent so many years waiting for each other.
We had to learn how to eat breakfast together and how to be silent in one room.
Now he keeps herbs on our balcony and talks to the basil as if it were a child.
Every evening we sit there, drink tea, and watch the lights come on across the city.
I have asked myself why our marriage lasted, and I think it was the letters.
Writing gave us time to think about what we wanted to say.
Ramon taught me that love is a daily practice, like cooking, and needs fresh ingredients.
He also taught me that a person can be far away and still beside you.
When I look at his hands now, they are spotted and a little shaky.
They are still the same hands that held my broken umbrella.
I would choose that rainy Sunday again without a moment of hesitation.
Even now, when thunder rolls over the city, he reaches for my hand.
I think a good marriage is mostly patience and a hot meal.
I moved to Abu Dhabi in nineteen ninety-two, and I remember the day I left Iloilo.
It was a hot morning in August, and my whole family came to the airport.
My mother held my face in her hands and told me not to forget how to cook rice.
My brothers carried my two suitcases, packed with clothes, books, and a bag of dried mangoes.
I was thirty-eight, and I had taught in the same school for fifteen years.
It was a hard decision, but the salary would help Liza and Paolo at school.
Ramon was at sea and could not come, so I cried on the phone the night before.
At the gate I saw my little niece waving a paper flag, and my heart nearly broke.
The airplane was enormous, and I held the armrests so tightly that my knuckles turned white.
Then I looked out at the clouds and felt I was floating over my whole life.
We landed in the middle of the night, and the airport air was thick with heat and dust.
A woman from the school was waiting with a card that spelled my name wrongly.
She drove me through quiet streets lit by orange lamps, past tall palm trees like sentries.
My apartment was small and bare, with a single bed, a kettle, and one window.
I sat on the bed and thought the silence was louder than the typhoon winds back home.
In the morning I walked to the school and met the principal, a tall Scottish lady.
My classroom had children from twenty countries, and I could not pronounce half their names.
But children are the same everywhere, curious and noisy and tender.
In the first weeks I was lonely, and I crossed off the days on a calendar.
I called home every Sunday from a phone booth, and the cards cost half my lunch money.
Slowly I found other Filipinos, and on Fridays we met at a church hall to share food.
A nurse named Amparo showed me which supermarket sold the right fish sauce.
The heat was a challenge, and I learned to carry a scarf and a bottle of water.
In summer the pavement felt like a stove, and everyone fled into the shade.
But winter evenings were gentle, and the desert air smelled of jasmine and the sea.
The city could be beautiful at sunset, when the towers turned pink.
My students taught me words in Arabic, Hindi, and Russian, and I taught them mabuhay.
Little by little the apartment became a home, with my sewing machine in the corner.
When the children joined me the following year, the place filled up with noise again.
Liza was thirteen, hated the heat, and cried at her first sandstorm.
Paolo was nine, and he thought the city was a giant playground with air conditioning.
I watched them grow up there, learning a new language of friendships and food.
Ramon visited between voyages, and he always brought me a small gift from a faraway port.
I started a church choir with six women, and now we are thirty voices.
After so many years I belong to two places at once.
In Iloilo I am a visitor with a foreign accent in the market.
Here I am the Filipino lady with the sewing basket and the loud laugh.
Moving teaches you that home is something you carry and rebuild.
I rebuilt mine from a kettle, a window, and the kindness of strangers.
Looking back, I am glad I was brave enough to board that airplane.
My mother would be proud, and I hope she knows I never forgot the rice.
The celebration I remember best is my daughter Liza's wedding, three years ago in Abu Dhabi.
It took a whole year to plan, and I was more nervous than the bride.
Liza married a gentle doctor named Daniel, whose family came from Kerala.
So we had two cultures and two kitchens at one table.
We held the ceremony in our church on a Friday evening in November.
I spent months sewing sixteen little gowns in yellow silk for the flower girls.
My fingers were sore, and I found pins in my cushions, my slippers, and once my sandwich.
Ramon was in charge of the food, and he cooked for four days with his brother.
They made a mountain of pancit for long life, because noodles must never be cut short.
There was also lechon, a whole roasted pig, which arrived in a van with its own driver.
Daniel's mother brought a huge pot of biryani, and the kitchens argued happily for hours.
On the wedding morning I woke before dawn and sat on the balcony with strong tea.
The sky was soft peach, the city was silent, and time seemed to hold its breath.
When I helped Liza into her gown, my hands trembled so much I could barely fasten the buttons.
She looked at me in the mirror, and I saw the little girl under my sewing table.
Her veil was made from my own mother's lace, which I had carried across the sea.
My choir sang during the ceremony, and I stood among the sopranos with tears on my face.
I could hardly manage the high notes, but the others carried me along.
Ramon walked Liza down the aisle in a gray suit, and his chin shook.
He whispered something to her, and later she told me it was a promise.
After the vows we stepped outside under a shower of rice and paper flowers.
The children ran in circles, and one little boy fell asleep under a table.
The reception was in a garden strung with golden lights and scented with jasmine.
My friends from the choir sang a surprise song, an old Filipino love song.
Then came the karaoke, which I had been waiting for all evening.
I took the microphone and sang a song Ramon had loved since our courting days.
He sat at the front table, watching me with his old, shy, sailor's smile.
Even Daniel's grandfather, a serious man who rarely spoke, stood up and clapped in rhythm.
We danced until the musicians were exhausted, and the cake looked like a battlefield.
Paolo made a speech and teased his sister so much that she threw a bread roll at him.
Everyone howled, and the photographer caught it, and that picture hangs in my hallway.
At the end of the party Liza kissed my forehead and thanked me for everything.
I could not speak, so I held her face the way my mother held mine.
The guests drifted away, and the staff began folding chairs and sweeping confetti.
Ramon and I sat on the steps with our shoes off and our feet aching beautifully.
He said the pig had been a triumph, and I said the bride had been one.
We agreed that both statements were true.
I have been to many celebrations, in villages and cities and even on ships.
But that night, with two families and two kitchens, felt like the whole world sitting down together.
Memory keeps the smells longer than it keeps the faces.
I hope that when I am very old, I still remember jasmine and roasted pig.
The teacher who influenced me most was Missus Ledesma, the principal of my first school.
She was tall and thin, with silver hair, and wore the same gray dress every Monday.
When I arrived at twenty-two, I was full of ideas and short on experience.
My first morning I wrote a long lesson plan on the board, and thirty children stared.
By ten o'clock half of them were asleep, and the others were drawing on their arms.
Missus Ledesma had stood at the back, and she waited until the bell rang.
Then she asked me gently whether I had looked at the children or only at my plan.
I was ashamed, but I knew she was right, because I had been teaching to the wall.
She invited me to her office, a tiny room with a battered desk and a pot of orchids.
She poured me hot calamansi juice and told me about her own terrible first day.
She had once been so nervous that she fainted into a bucket of chalk.
We laughed until we cried, and from then on I could ask her anything.
Over the next years she taught me to teach with my eyes, my hands, and my whole face.
She said a child can forgive a teacher almost anything except boredom.
She showed me how to turn a lesson about fractions into a story about sharing a cake.
We cut paper plates, and the children learned that half is not a quarter.
Once she brought a live crab to class so we could study how it walked sideways.
It escaped, and chaos followed, but I never forgot what a claw looks like.
She believed in noticing the quiet children, the ones who sat by the window.
She kept a little notebook and wrote one good thing about each child every week.
I copied that habit, and I have filled many notebooks over the decades.
When a boy named Ernesto could not read, she did not scold him or send him away.
She stayed after school with him for months, using flashcards made from cereal boxes.
By the end of the year Ernesto read aloud at the assembly, and half the audience wept.
I watched all this and learned that patience is the real engine of teaching.
Missus Ledesma was also strict about punctuality, tidy shelves, and polished shoes.
She said order gives children a sense of safety, and safety lets them be brave.
She never raised her voice, and her silence was more powerful than any shouting.
When I told her I planned to move abroad, she was quiet for a long time.
Then she took one orchid from the pot and said it should travel with me.
She wrapped it in damp newspaper, and I carried it in my handbag on the airplane.
It survived the flight and bloomed in my first apartment, a small purple miracle.
Missus Ledesma passed away a few years later, and I could not attend her funeral.
I lit a candle in my church in Abu Dhabi and sang her favorite hymn in the kitchen.
Many of the orchids on my balcony today are great grandchildren of that first plant.
Whenever a new bloom opens, I think of her gray dress and calm voice.
When I trained young teachers, I told them the story of the crab and the notebook.
Teaching is not about the plan on the board but about the faces in the room.
I hope that somewhere a child remembers me the way I remember her.
A good mentor does not hand you a map but teaches you to see the road.
I am grateful that she saw something in a nervous girl with a broken lesson plan.
The journey I have never forgotten happened when I was ten, on my father's boat.
My father had built a fishing boat for a man on Guimaras Island, across the strait.
He decided to deliver it himself, and to my surprise he asked me to come.
My brothers were jealous, but I was the one who always sat beside him in the workshop.
We left at dawn, with the sky streaked orange and the water flat as a mirror.
My mother packed rice, grilled fish, and a thermos of sweet coffee wrapped in a towel.
She gave me a straw hat and told me to behave like a lady and not a seagull.
The boat was painted bright blue, with a white stripe and a name on the bow.
It was called Maria Luisa, after the buyer's mother, and my father carved the letters himself.
I sat on a small bench at the front as the little engine coughed to life.
The wind smelled of salt and diesel, and the waves slapped the hull cheerfully.
Behind us Iloilo grew smaller, until the church towers looked like toys on a green tablecloth.
My father stood at the tiller, humming his old tune about the fisherman and the moon.
For the first time I saw him as a man at home on the water.
He pointed out a school of flying fish leaping across the surface like silver arrows.
I clapped so hard I nearly fell overboard, and he caught my dress.
He told me about the nights he had fished with only a lantern and a net.
He said the sea is like a good teacher, patient, severe, and generous all at once.
At midmorning a squall came up from the south, and the sky turned the color of slate.
The waves grew taller, and the little boat rocked until my stomach was near my ears.
My father calmly tied a rope around my waist and fastened it to the bench.
He told me to look at the horizon and sing, because singing children do not get sick.
So I sang every hymn I knew, shouting into the wind, and he joined in.
The rain came down in sheets, and we were soaked, laughing and shivering together.
After an hour the storm passed, and a rainbow stretched across the water.
I thought the whole world had been washed and was brand new.
We reached Guimaras by early afternoon, and a crowd was waiting on the beach.
The buyer, a short man in a straw hat, ran into the surf and kissed the bow.
His wife gave us grilled squid, steamed cassava, and mangoes as sweet as honey.
I ate until I could hardly move and fell asleep on a mat under a palm tree.
When I woke, the sun was low, and my father sat watching the sea with a quiet smile.
We returned on a crowded ferry, because the blue boat had stayed behind.
I leaned against my father's shoulder while the lights of Iloilo twinkled across the dark water.
He smelled of wood shavings and rain, and I felt entirely safe.
That day taught me that courage can be learned by singing in a storm.
It also taught me that a parent and child can share a whole world in one day.
My father has been gone for many years, but I still feel that rope around my waist.
Whenever I board a plane or a ferry, I hum his tune and watch the horizon.
I think that journey was the beginning of every adventure I have had since.
Maybe that is why I was never afraid to leave.
